draft.title: The budgeted income statement
card: A budgeted income statement estimates a business's revenue and expenses for the coming period. The difference is the budgeted profit or loss.
It is built on the accrual basis. Revenue is counted in the period it is earned, and expenses in the period they are incurred, whether or not cash changes hands.
So a credit sale made in the period is budgeted revenue, even if the customer pays next period. Expenses are budgeted when used, such as wages for work done in the period.
Some cash items are not income statement items. Buying equipment or repaying a loan is not an expense. Depreciation is an expense, even though it uses no cash.
draft.remember: A budgeted income statement estimates profit by matching revenue earned with expenses incurred, not cash received and paid.

a.q: Mia's café in Geelong expects to sell $6000 of catering on credit in June. Customers will pay in July. How is this treated in the June budgeted income statement?
opts: It is budgeted as June revenue
It is budgeted as July revenue
It is left out until the cash arrives
It is budgeted as a June expense
a.why: On the accrual basis, revenue is counted when it is earned, so the credit sale is June revenue. Counting it in July would follow the cash received, which is not the basis used for an income statement.
a.clue: Revenue is counted when it is earned, not when it is paid.

b.q: Dev's gym in Bendigo budgets to buy $20000 of new equipment in March, paid in cash. It will use $2000 of the equipment's value in the year. What goes in the budgeted income statement?
opts: Neither, because no expense is incurred
b.why: Buying equipment is not an expense, so the $20000 is left out. The $2000 of value used up is depreciation, which is an expense even though it uses no cash. Counting the $20000 would follow the cash paid.
b.clue: Which part of the equipment is used up in the period?

a.best: It is budgeted as June revenue
